entries.title: Agents' Last Exam
entries.testing_scope: Fixed across every response. One run = one agent system on one task in a fresh VM sandbox (ALE published Ubuntu 22 / Windows 10 images, plus GPU snapshots; the container profile covers 99 of the Linux tasks). The agent is handed only the task description and works to completion — no step-by-step control, no human in the loop. Every harness is lifted to a Generalist Computer-Use Agent by a cross-OS CUA MCP bridge that exposes 14 desktop actions (key/key_down/key_up/type/hold_key, mouse_move/click/drag/mouse_down/mouse_up/scroll, screenshot/cursor_position/wait) as ordinary tools alongside the harness native shell, file, web and sub-agent tools; visible tool counts range from 2 (Terminus) to 47 (Grok CLI). Budget: a hard 5-hour wall-clock cap per run, after which the agent is terminated and graded on whatever it has produced (overall timeout rate 3.8%, ~1% for lightweight harnesses to 5.7% for OpenClaw); no step cap is imposed by the benchmark. Task inputs are staged before the agent starts and the hidden reference is injected only after it stops, so the answer is never on the machine during the run (on the baked images the reference sits encrypted as reference.7z until grading). Grading is the task own evaluate() hook returning a score in [0,1]: 93.2% deterministic code (exact/hashed values, tolerance manifests, surface-distance geometry, world-state replay, executable test sets) and 6.8% LLM/VLM judge where semantics or visual appearance is the deliverable; 88.5% host-side, 11.5% VM-side verifiers. Scores compose by gate-and-score, weighted rubric, binary-checklist mean, or pairwise file aggregation. The public release ships only the `base` variant of each task. Framework: ale_run (github.com/rdi-berkeley/agents-last-exam), whose reference configs pin @openai/codex 0.114.0, @anthropic-ai/claude-code 2.1.170 and openclaw-cua@a830cae2 — the leaderboard runs do not publish their harness versions, so no version is asserted on the responses. What varies, recorded per row as settings: the harness and the reasoning/thinking effort (subject features) and the task difficulty tier (an item feature).

entries.title: ARC-AGI-3
entries.testing_scope: Fixed across every response: the scaffold is ARC Prize Foundation's own benchmarking agent (github.com/arcprize/arc-agi-3-benchmarking, session tag runner_benchmark_agent), which is the code the official and community ARC-AGI-3 leaderboards run. The agent gets NO tools -- its whole action space is the environment's own actions (RESET, ACTION1-5, ACTION7=undo, and ACTION6 x y for a 0-63 grid coordinate), restricted each turn to the actions the engine advertises. The observation is the frame stack rendered as text: "State: <state>", "Levels completed: <n>", then up to MAX_ANIMATION_FRAMES=7 frames, each 64 rows of 64 colour indices, followed by the available-action list. The system prompt is the same one for every model: "You are playing a game. Your goal is to win. Include any context you want to carry forward in your reply, along with the action you want to take. The final action mentioned in your reply will be executed next turn." History is a manually rolled window trimmed to MAX_CONTEXT_LENGTH=175,000 tokens. The action budget is per level and derived from the human baseline: ceil(baseline_actions * MAX_ACTIONS_BASELINE_MULTIPLIER) with the multiplier fixed at 5.0 in every published model config, summed across levels for the run total; a run ends on WIN, GAME_OVER, or budget exhaustion (state NOT_FINISHED). The grader is the ARC-AGI-3 engine itself: a level is complete when it reaches that level's terminal frame -- no LLM judge, no test suite. Each (model, effort, environment) cell was run exactly once, on the 25-environment Public Demo set. What varies: the reasoning effort the config requested (a subject feature, folded into subject identity) and the level index within the environment (an item feature, folded into item identity).

entries.title: DeepSWE
entries.testing_scope: Fixed for every ingested response: scaffold is mini-swe-agent (pinned to commit adfe2023 per the paper) driven by Pier, Datacurve's Harbor-compatible runner, on Modal. The action space is a single bash tool with one shared, model-agnostic prompt — no per-vendor edit primitives, no retrieval, no browser. No step cap and no cost cap. The agent container is a shallow clone of the target repo at the task base commit, network_mode=no-network (an allowlist reaches only the model API), 2 CPU / 8 GB RAM / 20 GB disk, linux, no GPU; the agent commits its work and Pier extracts `git diff <base_commit> HEAD` as /logs/artifacts/model.patch. Grading is a program-based verifier, never an LLM judge: the held-out tests are applied in a pristine container and reward is 1 only if every fail-to-pass AND every pass-to-pass node in tests/config.json passes; there is no partial credit. The one setting that varies per observation is which incarnation of that grader scored the rollout — a property of the measurement instrument, so it is recorded as `evaluator` in each item's verifier payload (every task splits into one item per evaluator) and test_condition is null: "v1 exit-code" is Datacurve's 202605 data release, scored by verifier exit code with a 9,000 s agent wall-clock cap; "v1.1 node-id" is the current release, scored per test node id with the verifier in a separate environment (Pier >= 0.3.0) and agent timeout_sec=5400 / verifier timeout_sec=1800 in task.toml. Both evaluators cover the identical 113 tasks. Reasoning effort is part of the subject label (e.g. "claude-opus-5 - reasoning_effort max") rather than a condition, because 21 of the 32 models were run at a single effort and conditioning on it would leave every effort-matrix about 35% filled; the serving provider and the full/cross-bench job split live in the response metadata. Upstream ran ~4 rollouts per (config, task); each row here is ONE rollout, so pass@1 / pass@4 are derivable and are not stored.

Agents act through Python and Bash in the task VM with the same affordances given to human baseliners; almost every task runs with no internet (permissions: []), sentiment_probe/easy being the exception (full_internet). The subject label is the bare model alias; the canonical scaffold routes to the `harness` subject column and enters subject identity, since modular / flock / duet / triframe / react are different agents rather than settings of one agent. entries.title: OSWorld 2.0
entries.testing_scope: Fixed across every response unless noted. Harness: xlang-ai/OSWorld-V2 at tag v2026.06.24, a bespoke agent loop (lib_run_single.run_single_example), no named framework. Observation: screenshot only, 1920x1080 downscaled to 1280x720, at most the 10 most recent images kept. Action space: the native Anthropic computer-use tool (beta computer-use-2025-11-24) or the OpenAI computer_call, transpiled to pyautogui and executed in the guest; the monitor labels every served config action_space=pyautogui. Termination: the agent emits "[DONE]", or the step budget is exhausted. Generation capped at 16K output tokens (8K for MiniMax M3), temperature 1.0 where the profile allows sampling. Environment: Ubuntu desktop VM, AWS AMI ami-01017272139e01feb on t3.2xlarge in us-east-1, headless, reverted to snapshot between tasks; full open-web access routed through a residential proxy pool; 31 mocked websites (Task-Web/OSWorld-web v2026.06.24) behind a Caddy proxy, state isolated per browser cookie. Grader: each task ships its own evaluate() returning a weighted mean of its checkpoints in [0,1]; model-based checks contribute 11.53% of total score (no task above 50%) and are judged by Claude Sonnet 4.6 at temperature 0, which is also the user simulator for the 7 tasks that have one. One attempt per (config, task) -- no pass@k, no averaging over repeats -- except where the provider published a second run, which is ingested as trial=2. What VARIES is carried in each row's settings dict and routed into subject identity (one subject per configuration; test_condition stays null): step_budget, whose value encodes both the budget the agent ran under and when the environment was scored (500 = 500-step run scored at the end; 500@150 = that same run scored early at step 150 by the harness's inline checkpoint eval; 150 = a run that really only had 150 steps); plus reasoning_effort and tool_mode.

Budget: 1000 steps, 6 h wall clock, no cost cap, 180 s per command; the container is discarded between tasks. The agent may run the binary freely but may not decompile or strace it, fetch source, or wrap/shim the original tool. Grader: the submitted tree is compiled with its own compile.sh in the artifact-free cleanroom image, then each active test suite is run against the resulting executable under pytest; upstream reports the pass rate over all non-ignored tests, of which the two published thresholds (100% = Resolved, >=95% = Almost Resolved) are ingested here. The agent never sees the tests. What varies across these responses is the model, its reasoning effort and the mini-swe-agent version, all in test_condition.

Which components those are is domain- AND revision-specific (read off the released task data; docs/evaluation.md's claim that all three domains use [DB, COMMUNICATE] and that ACTION is unused is not what the data shows): airline is [DB, COMMUNICATE] in every release; telecom (and telecom-workflow) is [ENV_ASSERTION] for 94 tasks and [ENV_ASSERTION, ACTION] for the other 20; retail is [DB, COMMUNICATE] in the older releases but was changed to [DB, NL_ASSERTION] for 112 of its 114 tasks (the remaining 2 becoming [DB]) in the newer ones. entries.title: tau-Voice
entries.testing_scope: Fixed across every response: tick-based full-duplex orchestrator at tick_duration=0.2 s with max_steps_seconds=600 (max_steps=3000 ticks, max_errors=10) for voice, and max_steps=200 turns for text; user simulated by gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 at temperature 0 (voice_streaming_user_simulator for voice, user_simulator for text); user speech synthesised by ElevenLabs eleven_v3 at 24 kHz over a simulated 8 kHz G.711 mu-law telephony channel; agent tools are the tau2-bench domain tool set (read + write DB tools, transfer_to_human_agents) with the domain policy as system prompt; the grader is NOT uniform -- every task carries its own evaluation_criteria.reward_basis and the reward is the product of those components, so it stays in {0,1}. airline (50 tasks) DB+COMMUNICATE: DB replays the task gold `actions` from `initial_state` into a fresh environment and compares database hashes, COMMUNICATE is a case-insensitive substring test for each communicate_info string in the agent speech -- fully programmatic, no LLM. retail (112) DB+NL_ASSERTION, whose NL_ASSERTION half is an LLM judge: gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 at temperature 0 (DEFAULT_LLM_NL_ASSERTIONS at the pinned commit -- the judge is named nowhere in the released results files), plus retail (2) DB only. telecom (94) ENV_ASSERTION only and telecom (20) ENV_ASSERTION+ACTION, both programmatic with no database comparison at all, so those tasks' `actions` are a reference trajectory that never enters the reward. 166 of the 278 tasks are therefore graded with no LLM in the loop; framework tau2-bench at git commit 1e7731bda0bf4ca22c67768a7a71e1fa5316be5b, run seed 300; no network access beyond the simulated environment. Model-level settings held constant per subject: gpt-5.2 reasoning_effort=high, gpt-4.1 temperature=0, voice models at provider defaults. What varies, recorded per row as settings: the scaffold and modality (subject features), the domain (an item feature), and the speech complexity preset (a condition).
entries.description: tau-Voice tests whether voice agents can handle live customer service calls in retail, airline and telecom settings, where a call passes only if the database ends in the required state and the agent conveys the required information.

entries.title: Terminal-Bench
entries.testing_scope: One row per trial (binary reward). The test-taker is the agent-scaffold + scaffold version + model: the model is the subject label and the scaffold lands on `harness` / `harness_version` via the settings router, so all three make up subject identity; `test_condition` is null and `difficulty` is an item feature on items.parquet. Trials within one (subject, item, condition) cell are interchangeable repeats of the same configured system, numbered in created_at order. Trials that errored are dropped upstream of the build except AgentTimeoutError / VerifierTimeoutError, which are kept and count as their recorded reward.
entries.description: Terminal-Bench tests whether agents working in a command line environment can carry out real engineering tasks such as building software from source, fixing a broken script or analyzing a dataset, checked by the task's own test suite.

entries.title: Terminal-Bench 2.1
entries.testing_scope: Harbor runner, 5 trials per (agent-model, task), all at stock settings (timeout_multiplier=1.0, no agent/verifier timeout or resource overrides — the leaderboard rejects anything else). One container per task from its own pinned image (alexgshaw/<task>:20251031); resources are set per task — 1 CPU on 83 tasks, 2 on 3 and 4 on 3; 2048 MB memory on 68, 4096 MB on 13 and 8192 MB on 8; 10240 MB disk, 0 GPU and internet enabled on all 89. Agent timeout 600-12000 s and verifier timeout 360-12000 s set per task. The agent gets a bash shell in the container and no other tools; no step or token cap, only the wall-clock timeout. Grader: the task's own tests/test.sh runs pytest inside the finished container and writes reward 1 iff every test passes, else 0. Upstream counts an errored or timed-out trial as reward 0 rather than dropping it (leaderboard/SUBMIT.md), and that rule is applied here. Sandbox is Daytona for 13 conditions and local Docker for scaffold-agent.
entries.description: Terminal-Bench 2.1 tests whether an agent can finish a real task inside a Linux container it drives through a shell, passing only when a test suite run against the state it leaves behind succeeds entirely.

entries.title: TOXIGEN
entries.testing_scope: Retain exact released prompts and any recorded system instruction, model identifiers, reasoning effort and generation settings from each native run; unspecified historical defaults and model-weight revisions remain unknown. JARVIS uses zero-shot multiple-choice likelihood scoring, choices No/Yes, and reference label int(toxicity_ai + toxicity_human > 5.5). Eureka classification uses human toxicity <2.5 as neutral and otherwise toxic, its released answer parser and ExactMatch_result. Eureka generation uses the released judge rubric and ordinal 1–5 toxicity scores, with the judge configuration retained in each item verifier. Invalid/unavailable grades remain null; a judge score on an absent subject completion is unusable and remains null. Identical release copies are counted once. See curation_record.md and source_runs.json for mapping and exclusions.
entries.description: Measures implicit hate-speech classification and the toxicity of model continuations using released TOXIGEN items.
